blocks.text: Words are the OS of Thought: George Lakoff Reveals the True Identity of Metaphor
Have you recently argued with someone, refuted them, or perhaps found yourself on the defensive?
If so, please stop and think for a moment.
Why do we use war terms like refute, defensive, attack, win, and lose when talking about the intellectual activity of argumentation?
An argument is not a fistfight. It is an exchange of words.
Yet, we subconsciously perceive argumentation as war.
Cognitive linguist George Lakoff points out the following in his book Metaphors We Live By.
"Metaphor is not just a decoration of words. It is the operating system of thought itself by which we understand the world."
Today, I will introduce the theory of Conceptual Metaphor, which is essential for creators to make intuitive designs.
1. Argument is War
The most famous example Lakoff gives is the metaphor that Argument is War.
Whether in English or Japanese, we borrow terms from war when talking about arguments.
I attacked his claim.
I defended my position.
That opinion has weak defenses.
I won the argument.
According to Lakoff, this is not just a figure of speech.
We understand the abstract act of arguing by fitting it into the structure of the concrete act of war.
That is why, in actual arguments, we regard the other person as an enemy, try to take territory, and try to decide the winner and loser.
What if we had another metaphor that Argument is Dance?
Perhaps the goal would be to cooperate with the partner to derive a beautiful conclusion, and the concept of winning or losing itself would disappear.
In other words, depending on which metaphor we adopt, our perception of reality and our actions themselves change.
2. Thought Born from the Body
So, where do these metaphors come from?
Lakoff's answer is simple. They come from our Body.
For example, there is a metaphor that Happy is Up, and Sad is Down.
We say feeling up, high spirits, feeling down, or sinking.
Why is good up and bad down in many languages around the world?
It is because humans are upright animals.
When we are healthy, our backs stretch and our posture becomes good, which is up. When we approach sickness or death, we collapse to the ground, which is down.
Another interesting example is the metaphor that Understanding is Digesting.
In Japanese, when we fully understand something, we say it falls into the intestines, or Fu ni Ochiru.
When we cannot accept something, we say we cannot swallow it.
In English, too, we use the phrase Gut feeling for intuition.
Actually, there is a philosophical ancestor to this idea. It is the French philosopher Maurice Merleau-Ponty.
While Descartes famously said, I think, therefore I am, separating the mind from the body, Merleau-Ponty argued, I am my body.
He claimed that our perception is not a camera-like input, but a physical interaction between the body and the world.
Lakoff inherited this philosophical baton and proved it with the lens of modern linguistics.
3. UI Design is Metaphor Design
This theory becomes the strongest weapon in game development and UI design.
This is because excellent UI is nothing but appropriate conceptual metaphor itself.
Look at your computer screen. There are the Desktop, Folders, and the Trash Can.
These are all analogies of the physical bodily experience of office work to the digital world. That is why we can use them intuitively without a manual.
Game UI is the same.
Why does the screen turn red when HP, or Hit Points, decrease? That is because of the metaphor that Life is Blood.
If the screen turned blue when HP decreased, players would intuitively misunderstand that they are freezing or that their MP decreased.
A creator's job is nothing other than linking new rules and functions to the bodily memories users already possess, that is, choosing the correct metaphor.
4. The Link with Affordance
Some of you might have noticed a connection with the concept of Affordance.
That intuition is sharp.
James Gibson argued that the environment creates possibilities for action, or affordances, through the body.
Lakoff argues that the body creates possibilities for thought through metaphor.
Especially in the digital world, these two are inseparable.
On a screen, there are no physical objects to grab or push.
However, by using the metaphor of a Button, we feel the affordance of pushing.
By using the metaphor of a Trash Can, we feel the affordance of throwing away.
Metaphor is the bridge that brings physical affordance into the digital world.
5. Conclusion: New Metaphor, New Reality
Lakoff says the following.
"New metaphors have the power to create a new reality."
If you are trying to make a new game or service that has never existed before, please look for a metaphor before explaining the functions.
Is it War? Or is it Dance?
Is it a Journey? Or is it Architecture?
When an appropriate metaphor is found, users should intuitively understand the complex world you created as nostalgically as their own garden.
The shape of the world changes with just one choice of words.
